evidence: src/application/order-service.ts: place() creates an Order, calls this.stock.reserve(order.lines), saves through the OrderRepository port and returns toOrderDto(order). This is use-case orchestration.
src/application/order-service.ts: advance() and cancel() hand state changes to the domain (order.advance(status), order.cancel()) instead of applying transition rules themselves.
src/application/order-service.ts: requireOrder() throws the domain NotFoundError when an order is missing. This is application-level handling, with no HTTP status mapping.
src/application/order-service.ts: persistence goes only through the OrderRepository and ProductRepository interfaces. The file has no storage or transport code.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: OrderService does the work of an application-layer use-case service. Each method loads an aggregate through a domain repository port, calls domain behaviour on it (Order constructor, order.advance, order.cancel, StockReservationService.reserve/release), saves it through the port, and maps the result to a DTO. The business rules sit in domain objects: status transitions in Order.advance and Order.cancel, and stock logic in StockReservationService. The file contains no persistence code (no SQL, ORM or storage calls), no transport code (no HTTP, request/response handling or status codes) and no framework wiring. Generating the ID with randomUUID and throwing NotFoundError when an order is missing are normal application-level jobs. The service builds StockReservationService itself instead of having it injected. That is a dependency-injection style choice, not a responsibility from another layer.
